source.title_on_document: The impact of Midjourney on students' design and design process: an exploratory study

supplement.holds: The paper mentions no supplementary material. It prints no tables and no statistics; results are narrative only.

paper_design_summary: Three consecutive yearly cohorts of master's students in interior architecture (retail design) at Hasselt University did the same concept-store design exercise. The 2022-2023 cohort (6 students) used no AI; the 2023-2024 cohort (11 students) was taught Midjourney in the store development phase; the 2024-2025 cohort (6 students) was taught Midjourney in the concept development phase. The two teachers assessed final designs on innovativeness, originality, and creativity and tracked process timing; no scores or statistics are printed.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Whether and when Midjourney was taught: none (2022-2023 cohort), in the store development phase (2023-2024 cohort), or in the concept development phase (2024-2025 cohort). Each academic-year cohort received one condition.
assignment.quote: The study was conducted among Master students of interior architecture majoring in retail design in the academic year 2022-2023, 2023-2024 and 2024-2025, with 2022_2023 as the control group, using no AI.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 153), Section 2 Experimental set-up

arms.name: Group 1 (2022-2023, control)
arms.description: No Midjourney taught or mentioned; end-of-exercise survey found students unfamiliar with Midjourney or any other AI design tool.

arms.name: Group 2 (2023-2024, Midjourney in store development phase)
arms.description: Midjourney taught in a half-day session and introduced in the store development phase, after the concept phase.

arms.name: Group 3 (2024-2025, Midjourney in concept development phase)
arms.description: Midjourney taught in a half-day session at the beginning of the design process, during the concept development phase.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or total analyzed N are reported. The arm counts are the printed cohort sizes (6, 11, and 6), not separately reported analysis denominators (PDF p. 4, printed p. 153, Section 2; PDF p. 8, printed p. 157, Section 6).
participants.who: Master's students of interior architecture majoring in retail design, Hasselt University, three academic-year cohorts.
participants.quote: During the first year of the three (2022-2023), no Midjourney was taught nor mentioned to the 6 students following the master (group 1). [...] Midjourney was taught to 11 students [...] This year, there were 6 students involved.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 153), Section 2 Experimental set-up; sample size also in Section 6 Limitations, PDF p. 8 (printed p. 157): '6-11 students per year'

ai_tool.how_used: Text-to-image generation to create and iterate concept boards (Group 3) or to recreate concept boards and seek inspiration during store development (Group 2); half-day training with two hands-on exercises.

task.description: Design a concept store for an internationally recognized luxury brand or designer (student's choice, e.g. Louis Vuitton, Dolce & Gabbana, Rolex) within a 400 m2 space, with a focus on an immersive shopping experience; individual projects.
task.duration: Group 1: seven weeks of initial research and analysis followed by another seven weeks of design; Group 2 followed the same timeline. Group 3: analysis and concept development took less time, reducing the need for the additional one to two weeks typically required to make a concept board manually; no complete Group 3 duration is reported (PDF p. 7, printed p. 156, second Section 4.2, Impact on design process).

outcomes.name: Creativity of the final design (depth and meaningfulness of ideas, strength of conceptual storytelling)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Qualitative assessment by the two teachers (a retail design expert and the author) of student designs, workflow documents, and presentations against a predetermined 'creativity' criterion; no scores, rubric, or statistics printed.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Group 3 (2024-2025, Midjourney in concept development phase)
contrasts.reported: "there was a noticeable increase in the creativity factor, particularly in Group 3." No numbers printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 156), Section 4.2 Impact on final design

outcomes.name: Innovativeness of the final design
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Qualitative assessment by the two teachers against a predetermined 'innovativeness' criterion (new and forward-thinking solutions); no scores or statistics printed.

contrasts.reported: "An analysis of the students' results revealed no significant impact on two of the three predetermined evaluation criteria: innovativeness and originality." No numbers printed; 'significant' is not backed by any test.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 156), Section 4.2 Impact on final design

outcomes.name: Originality of the final design (uniqueness compared to existing market solutions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Qualitative assessment by the two teachers against a predetermined 'originality' criterion; no scores or statistics printed.

contrasts.reported: "the extent to which the designs introduced new solutions, and their uniqueness compared to existing designs remained relatively consistent across all groups." No numbers printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 156), Section 4.2 Impact on final design

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 not met: the conditions follow three successive academic-year cohorts (2022-2023 control, 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 Midjourney), not random assignment (PDF p. 4, printed p. 153, Section 2). Criterion 2 not met: the reported cohort sizes of 6, 11, and 6 students place the study below the 50-person threshold; no total analyzed N or exclusions are reported (PDF p. 4, Section 2; PDF p. 8, printed p. 157, Section 6). Criterion 3 met: student designs were evaluated on innovativeness, originality, and creativity (PDF p. 5, printed p. 154, Section 3; PDF p. 7, printed p. 156, first Section 4.2). The assessments are qualitative, with no numerical scores or statistics printed. Context class observational: people compared under non-random assignment.

one_line_finding: Across three yearly cohorts of 6, 11, and 6 master's retail design students (PDF p. 4, printed p. 153, Section 2), the qualitative assessment described increased creativity particularly in the cohort introduced to Midjourney during concept development, while innovativeness and originality remained relatively consistent across groups, with no numerical outcome scores or statistical tests reported (PDF p. 7, printed p. 156, first Section 4.2).
notes: Locators give the PDF page first (page 1 is the DRS cover sheet) and the printed page in parentheses. Process timing is not recorded as a creativity outcome: Group 1 spent seven weeks on research and analysis followed by seven weeks on design, and Group 2 followed the same timeline. Group 3's analysis and concept development took less time, reducing the need for the additional one to two weeks typically required to make a concept board manually; no complete Group 3 duration is reported (PDF p. 7, printed p. 156, second Section 4.2, Impact on design process; the paper numbers two sections 4.2). The abstract describes early-stage development as reduced by 1-2 weeks (PDF p. 2, printed p. 151). The semester-long project mentioned on PDF p. 5 (printed p. 154, continuation of Section 2) was an earlier bachelor's project. All 188 markdown lines and all 9 PDF pages were read, including the limitations, references, author biography, and license. No tables or appendices appear in this PDF; no supplement is mentioned.
